messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Somchai, a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian fisherman, came to treatment after months of feeling unable to settle since the day a storm took his younger brother from him. He and his brother had gone out before dawn in their small boat, as they had done for years, checking the nets off the coast while the village was still dark and quiet. The weather turned faster than expected, the waves rose hard against the hull, and in the confusion Somchai watched his brother lose his footing and disappear into the black water. By the time rescue teams searched the area, there was nothing they could do. Since then, Somchai has carried the memory of that morning like a weight that never fully leaves him. He speaks of it in a flat, distant way, saying he feels dead inside, as if some essential part of him stayed out at sea with his brother. He also says that surviving when his brother did not feels wrong, and the guilt has hardened into a kind of private punishment.

In the months that followed, Somchai began to see other people differently. He came to believe that people cannot be trusted, because the sea, the weather, and even the warnings from others had all seemed unreliable that morning, and no one had been able to protect his brother. That mistrust widened beyond the event itself. He stopped relying on crew members the way he used to, watched faces carefully for signs that someone might be careless or hiding something, and found himself assuming that if he let his guard down, something else terrible would happen. At the same time, the sight and sound of reminders in daily life started to hit him hard. When he heard a sudden gust of wind rattling the tin roof at home, or saw dark water slap against the harbor wall while unloading nets in the early morning, his chest would tighten, his heart would pound, and his body would react before he could think. He became intensely watchful around storms and rough weather, bracing himself as though danger were already returning. What frightened him most was not only the memory of losing his brother, but the thought that the world was still the same unsafe place that had taken him away.

Those physical surges fed back into his beliefs about the world. Each time his body reacted so strongly, Somchai took it as proof that he had not left the danger behind and that he could not trust anything around him to be safe. The more his hands shook and his breathing shortened when clouds gathered over the water, the more certain he became that vigilance was the only thing keeping him from being caught off guard again. In that sense, the very sensations that alarmed him made his mistrust feel reasonable and necessary, as if his body were confirming what his mind already feared. He began sleeping badly, lying awake long after his wife had turned off the lamp, listening for weather changes and replaying the moment his brother slipped from sight. When he did sleep, it was light and broken, and he woke tense and drained.

Over time, Somchai avoided the parts of his work that brought the memory closest. He stayed closer to shore when he could, let others handle the rougher trips, and hesitated whenever the forecast hinted at wind. The changes strained him at work and at home, because fishing had always been tied to identity, routine, and family life. He did not say much about his distress to his wife, but she noticed how withdrawn he had become and how often he sat silently after returning from the harbor. Somchai himself described that silence as emotional numbness, though it felt less like calm than like being sealed off from everyone else. Even when others tried to comfort him, he could not fully take it in. Instead he kept turning back to the same conclusion: if he trusted too easily, if he relaxed for even a moment, he might be punished again by losing someone else.

By the time he sought help, Somchai was exhausted by the constant strain of feeling on edge and ashamed of surviving. He had finally come because the nights had become too long and the sea too difficult to face each morning, and he was afraid that his body would keep reacting this way forever. He hoped therapy might help him sleep and lessen the surges of fear and anger that still rise whenever weather, water, or a sudden noise brings his brother’s death back before him. More than anything, he wanted to believe that remaining alive did not mean he had failed his brother, and that trust might someday feel possible again.
